  1. Epidermis — the outer skin layer sitting UPON the dermis; the burn layer you assess first.
  2. Epigastric — the region OVER the stomach; epigastric pain can mean an MI, not just heartburn.
  3. Epiglottis — the flap ABOVE the glottis that shields the airway; it swells shut in epiglottitis.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Eupnea — normal, easy breathing; what you chart when respirations are calm and unlabored.
  2. Euglycemia — a normal blood glucose; the goal sitting between hypo- and hyperglycemia.
  3. Euthymia — a normal, stable mood; the psych baseline between depression and mania.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Exhalation — moving air OUT of the lungs; the passive phase of every breath you count.
  2. Exophthalmos — eyeballs bulging OUTward, the classic look of Graves' hyperthyroidism.
  3. Excision — cutting a lesion OUT; what a surgeon does to remove a suspicious mole.

Ex: extraneous = outside the organism and not belonging to it

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Extravasation — IV fluid or drug leaking OUTSIDE the vein into tissue; why you recheck a running line.
  2. Extracellular fluid — the fluid OUTSIDE the cells (plasma and interstitial); where your IV bolus first lands.
  3. Extraocular movements — eye motions run by muscles OUTSIDE the eyeball; you chart them as 'EOMI' on a neuro exam.

Ex: hemiplegia = paralysis on one side of the body

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Hemiplegia — paralysis of one HALF (one side) of the body; a hallmark of stroke.
  2. Hemithorax — one HALF of the chest; you note absent breath sounds in the left hemithorax with a pneumothorax.
  3. Hemicolectomy — surgical removal of HALF the colon, often for cancer or diverticulitis.

Ex: hyperventilation = fast ventilations

Distinguish: opposite is hypo- (under/below)

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Hypertension — HIGH blood pressure; the 'silent killer' vital you flag on nearly every reading.
  2. Hyperglycemia — excessively HIGH blood sugar; it drives DKA in a diabetic emergency.
  3. Hyperthermia — dangerously HIGH body temperature, as in heat stroke on a hot call.

Ex: hypoperfusion = below-normal blood flow to vital organs

Distinguish: opposite is hyper- (over/excessive)

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Hypoglycemia — blood sugar BELOW normal; a classic cause of altered mental status you fix with dextrose.
  2. Hypoxia — oxygen BELOW normal in the tissues; what a dropping pulse-ox is warning you about.
  3. Hypodermic — literally UNDER the skin; the hypodermic needle delivers a subcutaneous injection.

Text: The prefix {{c1::in-}} means {{c2::in, into, not, without}}.
Back Extra:
WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Inhalation — breathing air IN; the active phase of ventilation and a route for nebulized meds.
  2. Incision — a surgical cut INTO tissue; you dress and protect a fresh one as a wound.
  3. Incontinence — here in- flips to 'not': NOT able to control the bladder or bowel, common after a seizure or stroke.

Ex: infraclavicular = below the clavicle

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Infraorbital — BELOW the eye socket; the infraorbital rim is a key landmark when checking for facial fractures.
  2. Infraspinatus — the rotator-cuff muscle BELOW the scapular spine; a common shoulder-injury culprit.
  3. Infrarenal aorta — the aorta BELOW the kidney arteries, the usual site of an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

Distinguish: opposite is intra- (within)

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Intercostal muscles — the muscles BETWEEN the ribs; you watch for intercostal retractions in respiratory distress.
  2. Intervertebral disc — the cushion BETWEEN two vertebrae; it can herniate and pinch a nerve root.
  3. Interphalangeal joint — the joint BETWEEN finger bones; a common spot for a finger dislocation.

Ex: intrauterine = within the uterus

Distinguish: opposite is inter- (between)

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Intravenous (IV) — WITHIN a vein; the route for most fluids and emergency drugs you push.
  2. Intraosseous (IO) — WITHIN the bone; the drill-in access you use when you can't get an IV.
  3. Intracranial hemorrhage — bleeding WITHIN the skull; the rising intracranial pressure is a brain emergency.

Ex: ipsilateral = on or affecting the same side

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Ipsilateral blown pupil — a dilated pupil on the SAME side as an expanding brain bleed (CN III compression in herniation).
  2. Ipsilateral breath sounds — in a tension pneumothorax they're absent on the SAME side as the injury, while the trachea shifts away.
  3. Ipsilateral weakness — a spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Sequard) weakens the SAME side below the level of injury.

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Isotonic — an IV fluid with the same (equal) osmolarity as blood; normal saline and LR won't shift water across cells, making them your workhorse resuscitation fluids.
  2. Isocoria — equal pupil size, the normal finding you chart; its opposite, anisocoria, flags a head injury.
  3. Isoelectric line — equal (balanced) electrical charge, seen as the flat ECG baseline; asystole is a completely isoelectric line.

Distinguish: opposite is micro- (small)

WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
  1. Macrocytic anemia — red cells that are abnormally large (high MCV), classic for B12 or folate deficiency.
  2. Macrosomia — an abnormally large newborn (over 4 kg), which raises the risk of shoulder dystocia at delivery.
  3. Macrophage — the 'big eater' immune cell that engulfs bacteria and cellular debris.
